extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, novelists, and students of narrative craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and executing the narrative method (dramatic/scene-based vs pictorial/narrator-driven) appropriate to a novel's subject, including handling point of view, background, interiority, and consistency of method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a narrator only if the narrator is a value
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the presence of a seer and a recorder is made a value in itself, contributing definitely to the effect of the subject, he is better dispensed with and put out of the way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include an intrusive narrator for convenience. The narrator should be justified by the subject: if the story demands reflection, summary, or a particular standpoint, keep the narrator; otherwise prefer direct presentation. Anti-pattern: bringing a spokesman forward 'for the convenience of the author' when it does not aid the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct view when other things are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: Where other things are equal a direct view of the matter in hand is the best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject can be presented clearly and fully by dramatization or by letting events speak for themselves, choose that direct view rather than interposing an observing voice. Use narration only when it adds necessary value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match method to the subject (dramatic vs pictorial)
rubrics_metrics.description: A large, loose, manifold subject, extensive in time and space, full of crowds and diversions, is a pictorial subject and can be nothing else; a clean-cut situation raising a question of its issue is dramatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify your subject before choosing form: panoramas/chronicles (Thackeray, Balzac) generally require a narrator/summary; compact action-driven situations (The Awkward Age) suit pure dramatic, scene-by-scene treatment. Example: big chronicles need the chronicler to 'draw back for a general view'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy: the narrator as principle of economy
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator, standing in front of the story, represents the great principle of economy, and is a value in himself, and does contribute to the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a narrator can efficiently present wide span, summarize, or compress material economically, their presence is justified. Use narrator to avoid tedious scenic exposition when economy of presentation is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize interior life when possible (show thought through gesture)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story that is concerned with the impact of experience upon a mind ... can be enhanced to the pitch of drama, because thought has its tell-tale gestures and its speaking looks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where inner states can be externalized—via looks, gestures, 'tell-tale' behaviour—express them scenically rather than resort to exposition. Method upon method: let thought enact itself through observable signs. Example: Strether's imagination made dramatic by showing his gestures and looks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of method matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole of the book passes scenically before the reader... The novelist using this method claims only one advantage over the playwright ... Otherwise the novelist completely ties his hands, submitting to all the restraints of the playwright in order to secure the compactness and the direct force of true drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to pursue one dominant method (strict drama or pictorial/narrator) and maintain internal consistency. A sustained single method can create a distinctive and cohesive effect (example: The Awkward Age), but it is difficult and risky; only attempt it with good cause and skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial control over manner when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist ... creates the manner in which the words are spoken, as well as the words themselves, and he may keep the manner at an ideal pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the author wishes to fix not only what is said but how it is said (tone, precise delivery), the novelist's control can be an advantage over drama. Use this to ensure nuances of manner that actors might not convey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forcing vivid drama into narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes he actually embarrasses it, when a matter of vivid drama is violently forced into the form of a narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't neutralize immediacy by summarizing or commenting on scenes that would be stronger if presented directly. Anti-pattern: inserting retrospective exposition over an incident that should unfold in front of the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic method is narrow and may need supplement for background
rubrics_metrics.description: From the point of view of the reader, the dramatic scene is vivid and compact; but it is narrow, it can have no great depth, and the colour of the atmosphere can hardly tell within the space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the effect of the action depends on time, place, or wider social atmosphere, supplement dramatic scenes with pictorial or narrative material to establish setting and associations. Recognize drama's limitation in conveying outlying associations and plan accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictorial/background material to propulse action
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of the generalized picture, for example, supporting the play of action, ... becomes a kind of propulsive force applied to the action at the start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build setting and background deliberately (Balzac's method) so that when action begins it acts with reserve and momentum drawn from the prepared scene. Preparatory pictures can supply character and energy to subsequent drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether the action itself fully covers motives
rubrics_metrics.description: With the people of The Awkward Age, on the other hand, their action fully covers their motives and sentiments—or can be made to do so, by the care of a dexterous author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If characters' visible actions can convey motives and sentiments, omit interior exposition. If not, include appropriate narrative or reflective passages. Aim to make action expressive enough to imply interiority when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance freedom and restraint: use mixed method where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in dealing with a subject entirely dramatic, a novelist may well find reason to keep to his old familiar mixed method—circumspice; it would appear that he does so invariably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be pragmatic: strict adherence to one extreme is rare and difficult. Consider mixing dramatic scenes with narrative overview when the subject requires both immediacy and wider perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge whether the background must be explicitly shown
rubrics_metrics.description: Nanda and her case are not rendered if the quality of the civilization round her is left in any way doubtful ... For the purposes of her story it is important that her setting should be clearly seen and known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a story's effect depends on a very particular social milieu or background, ensure that setting is vividly rendered rather than merely implied. Anti-pattern: assuming readers will supply a complex background unaided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous cross-book associations that disturb unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the characters in the remoter planes of the action ... no more is expected than their value for the purpose of the action in the foreground. ... whatever more they may bring will lie idle, will contribute nothing, and may even become an embarrassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reusing characters or references from other works, include only associations relevant to the current story. Extraneous past associations can distract and confuse the reader, harming unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a subject is extensive in time/space, assign point of view to a narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: It is absolutely necessary for the author or his spokesman to draw back for a general view of the matter from time to time; and whenever he does so the story becomes his impression, summarized and pictured for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sprawling subjects with large temporal or spatial scope, plan periodic authorial or narrator perspective to consolidate and summarize large stretches that cannot be shown scenically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of the easy resort to omniscience
rubrics_metrics.description: It must always be simpler for a story-teller to use his omniscience, to dive into the minds of his people for an explanation of their acts, than to make them so act that no such explanation is ever needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist overuse of omniscient commentary merely for convenience. Strive to dramatize where possible; use omniscience deliberately and sparingly for effect or necessary summation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the cost/benefit of a tour de force of consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The beauty of its resolute consistency is of course a value in it, and it may be great enough to justify a tour de force. But a tour de force it is, when a novelist seeks to render the general life of his story in the particular action, and in the action alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If attempting an extreme formal experiment (e.g., pure drama throughout), weigh the artistic payoff against the difficulty and limitations, especially in conveying setting and background. Example: The Awkward Age as a successful tour de force; rare and demanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use description economically to create a scene that supports drama
rubrics_metrics.description: When Balzac takes in hand the description of a town or a house or a workshop, ... when he has finished his lengthy research among the furniture of the lives that are to be evoked, he has created a scene in which action will move as rapidly as he chooses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed descriptive work should be directed toward making the scene serve the action—gathering 'the daily experience' into an impression that deepens characters and supplies momentum. Avoid description 'for its own sake' unless it ultimately serves the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that some narrative habits persist from criticism and tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism seems to have paid it less attention than it deserves ... it is true, no doubt, that the novel ... is more than ever inclined to the big pictorial subject, which requires the voluble chronicler;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that critical and readerly expectations, as well as tradition, shape narrative choices. Understand when to conform to or challenge those habits, and be explicit about the reasons for doing so in service of effect.
